result.markdown: --- title: "Interpolation and kernels" engine: julia --- Convolution interpolation builds a function from data on a grid by placing a copy of a kernel at every knot, scaled by the data value there, and adding them up. The kernels are piecewise polynomials with compact support, and they are cardinal: one at their own knot, zero at every other. So the sum passes through the data, and between the knots it is a weighted combination of a fixed number of nearby values. This is the structure of a cubic spline too; the difference is that the kernels are designed, not solved for, and that lets the design go to much higher order while every evaluation stays local. The [theory page](../theory.qmd) derives the kernels from their defining conditions. ## A first example A sine sampled sparsely, interpolated with the default kernel, in both packages: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Julia ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = range(0, 2π, length = 8) # eight uniformly spaced samples y = sin.(x) # the values at the samples itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y) # the interpolant, default kernel :b7 xf = range(0, 2π, length = 400) # fine points for plotting plot(xf, sin.(xf), color = :black, label = "sin(x)") # the function being sampled plot!(xf, itp.(xf), label = "interpolant") # the interpolant between the samples scatter!(x, y, markershape = :circle, markercolor = :white, markerstrokewidth = 1.5, label = "samples") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from convinterp import convolution_interpolation x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 8) # eight uniformly spaced samples y = np.sin(x) # the values at the samples itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y) # the interpolant, default kernel "b7" xf = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 400) # fine points for plotting plt.plot(xf, np.sin(xf), "k", label="sin(x)") # the function being sampled plt.plot(xf, itp(xf), label="interpolant") # the interpolant between the samples plt.plot(x, y, "o", mfc="white", label="samples") # the samples themselves plt.legend() ``` The Python port gives the same values as the Julia package to the last bit, so the figure is the same. ::: Eight samples per period is a coarse sampling for a sine, and the interpolant is already close; the next section shows how the error falls as samples are added. The largest error of the interpolant on the fine points is 1.08e-02. ## The kernels The `kernel` keyword chooses the kernel. All of them are piecewise polynomials that pass through the data; they differ in accuracy, smoothness, how many derivatives and integrals they provide, and cost. "Continuity" is how many derivatives of the interpolant are continuous, and the stencil is how many data values each evaluated point combines. | Kernel | Degree | Continuity | Derivatives up to | Integrals up to | Convergence | Stencil in $N$ dimensions | |:--|--:|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--| | `:a0` | 0 | — | — | 2 | 1st order | $2^N$ | | `:a1` | 1 | $C^0$ | — | 2 | 2nd order | $2^N$ | | `:a3` | 3 | $C^1$ | 1 | 4 | 3rd order | $4^N$ | | `:a4` | 3 | $C^1$ | 1 | 4 | 4th order | $6^N$ | | `:a5` | 5 | $C^3$ | 1 | 4 | 3rd order | $6^N$ | | `:a7` | 7 | $C^5$ | 1 | 4 | 3rd order | $8^N$ | | `:b5` | 5 | $C^3$ | 3 | 6 | 6th order | $10^N$ | | `:b7` | 7 | $C^5$ | 5 | 8 | 7th order | $12^N$ | | `:b9` | 9 | $C^7$ | 6 | 8 | 7th order | $14^N$ | | `:b11` | 11 | $C^9$ | 7 | 8 | 7th order | $16^N$ | | `:b13` | 13 | $C^{11}$ | 7 | 8 | 7th order | $18^N$ | In Python the kernels are strings, `"b7"` instead of `:b7`. The convergence order follows from the polynomials a kernel reproduces exactly: a kernel that reproduces polynomials up to degree $m$ converges at order $m + 1$ as the spacing shrinks. Some guidance: - **`:b7` is the default in 1D and 2D**, and the right choice for most smooth data: 7th-order convergence and five continuous derivatives. - **`:b7` to `:b13` all converge at 7th order.** The wider kernels are not more accurate; they are smoother and provide higher derivatives. Choose `:b9` to `:b13` when you need those. - **`:b5` converges at 6th order** with a smaller stencil, which makes it the default in 3D. - **`:a4` is a fast 4th-order kernel**, comparable to a cubic spline, and `:a1` is linear interpolation. `:a5` and `:a7` are smoother than `:a3` but converge at the same 3rd order. - **`kernel = :auto`**, the default, chooses by the number of dimensions, to keep the stencil affordable: `:b7` up to 2D, `:b5` in 3D, `:a4` in 4D and 5D, and `:a3` beyond. ## Convergence The orders in the table are what the error does as samples are added, once the grid resolves the function. The test function is Runge's, $1 / (1 + 25x^2)$ on $[-1, 1]$, whose narrow peak is the classical difficulty for polynomial interpolation. It is interpolated with four kernels on grids of increasing density, and the largest error between the samples is plotted against the spacing: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The convergence study"} runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2) # Runge's function xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001) # fine points for measuring the error kernels = (:a1, :a4, :b5, :b7) # linear, quartic, and the two high-order kernels ns = [11, 21, 41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281] # the numbers of samples, each grid refining the last hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1) # the corresponding spacings errors = [begin xn = range(-1, 1, length = n) # the samples itp_k = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = k) maximum(abs.(itp_k.(xr) .- runge.(xr))) # the largest error on the fine points end for n in ns, k in kernels] plot(xscale = :log10, yscale = :log10, xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error", legend = :bottomleft, xflip = true) for (j, k) in enumerate(kernels) plot!(hs, errors[:, j], marker = :circle, label = string(k)) end plot!(hs, errors[end, end] .* (hs ./ hs[end]) .^ 7, color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "slope 7") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | Kernel | Observed order | |:--|--:| | `a1` | 1.98 | | `a4` | 3.98 | | `b5` | 7.07 | | `b7` | 7.41 | On the coarsest grids every kernel is far from its order: the peak is a few samples wide, and no stencil can do better than the data allow. Once the grid resolves the peak the curves settle onto their slopes, and `:b7` reaches rounding first. The [interpolation benchmark](../benchmarks/interpolation.qmd) runs the same study against the other interpolation packages. ## Data in more dimensions For data on an $N$-dimensional grid, give one knot vector per axis as a tuple. Axis $d$ of the data array runs along knot vector $d$, so `data[i, j]` belongs to the point `(x[i], y[j])`. The kernels are applied along one axis at a time, so the interpolant in $N$ dimensions is a tensor product of the 1D kernels and inherits their convergence order: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Julia ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} xg = range(-1, 1, length = 12) # 12 knots along x yg = range(-1, 1, length = 10) # 10 knots along y field = [exp(-2 * (xi^2 + yi^2)) * cos(3xi) for xi in xg, yi in yg] # the data on the coarse grid itp2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), field) # the 2D interpolant xf2 = range(-1, 1, length = 200) # fine x values yf2 = range(-1, 1, length = 200) # fine y values fine = [itp2(xi, yi) for xi in xf2, yi in yf2] # the interpolant on the fine grid p1 = heatmap(xg, yg, field', title = "data, 12 × 10", aspect_ratio = 1, colorbar = false) p2 = heatmap(xf2, yf2, fine', title = "interpolant, 200 × 200", aspect_ratio = 1, colorbar = false) plot(p1, p2, layout = (1, 2), size = (800, 380)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python xg = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 12) # 12 knots along x yg = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 10) # 10 knots along y X, Y = np.meshgrid(xg, yg, indexing="ij") # coordinates, shape (12, 10) field = np.exp(-2.0 * (X**2 + Y**2)) * np.cos(3.0 * X) # the data on the coarse grid itp2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), field) # the 2D interpolant xf2 = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 200) # fine x values yf2 = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 200) # fine y values fine = itp2(xf2[:, None], yf2[None, :]) # a column against a row: shape (200, 200) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.8)) ax1.imshow(field.T, origin="lower", extent=(-1, 1, -1, 1)) # .T: imshow puts the first axis vertically ax1.set_title("data, 12 × 10") ax2.imshow(fine.T, origin="lower", extent=(-1, 1, -1, 1)) ax2.set_title("interpolant, 200 × 200") ``` In Python the coordinates broadcast like NumPy arrays, so a column of x values against a row of y values evaluates the whole table in one call. ::: The stencil sets the cost: in 3D, `:b7` combines $12^3 = 1728$ values per evaluated point, which is why the default narrows with the dimension. Evaluation never depends on the grid size, only on the stencil — locating the cell is one division per axis on a uniform grid. ## Where the data end Near the ends of the data the stencil reaches beyond the last knot. The packages fill those positions by extrapolating the data, polynomially where the data allow it, which keeps the full order up to the boundary; the [boundaries page](boundaries.qmd) shows the choices and when they matter.
